description: I'm a Computer Science student and AI/ML researcher with experience in software development, computer vision, and building interactive systems. I'm developing a space mission simulation game for the NASA Space Apps Challenge that combines scientific learning with engaging gameplay. I'm looking for teammates interested in game development, UI/UX design, 3D modelling, space science, and storytelling. Whether you're technical or creative, there's room to contribute!
summary:
Apogee Mission Studio is a browser-based, permanently 2D spaceflight game that connects spacecraft design with a complete Earth observation mission. Players assemble a craft from compatible parts, check its engineering readiness, and launch using manual controls or guided ascent assistance.

The simulation accounts for gravity, atmospheric drag, fuel consumption, and changing spacecraft mass. Live telemetry and an orbital map help players understand how their decisions affect flight. The science mission adds practical constraints: collect a daylight observation, manage solar power and battery reserves, and transmit data during ground-station contact within a deadline and budget.

We completed the core assembly, flight, and science mission milestones. Supporting features include undo and redo, independent zoom controls, time acceleration, local autosaving, session export/import, and a downloadable mission debrief. The verified reference mission returned 16 MB of data within its limits. Future work includes student playtesting, accessibility improvements, and expanded missions such as staging, landing, and rover exploration.
details:
Apogee Mission Studio is a browser-based, 2D spaceflight game designed to help secondary school students explore spacecraft engineering and orbital science through experimentation. Players assemble a spacecraft from compatible parts, check its readiness, and launch it using manual controls or guided ascent assistance. Gravity, atmospheric drag, fuel consumption, and changing mass affect its motion, while live telemetry and an orbital map explain the flight.

The game connects spacecraft design to a complete Earth observation mission. Players must collect data over a daylight target, manage battery power and solar generation, and transmit their observation during ground-station contact. They must succeed within a budget and deadline. A mission debrief explains the outcome through resource measurements and an event timeline, helping players connect their decisions with consequences.

We developed the project using TypeScript, Vite, HTML, CSS, and SVG graphics. Its creative approach combines spacecraft construction, flight simulation, and science operations in one continuous experience. Features include undo and redo, adjustable simulation speed, independent zoom controls, automatic saving, session import/export, and downloadable mission reports.

During development, we considered readable interfaces, keyboard controls, desktop and tablet layouts, consistent physics, and reliable resource accounting. Automated tests and browser checks verified the core mission. The intended impact is to make space engineering more approachable and encourage scientific reasoning through repeated experiments. Student learning benefits remain a goal to evaluate through future playtesting.
